customer_question: Our quote request lists a particular Controller Subsystem QDID and a particular Host Stack + Profile QDID for this registration -- are these the right ones to reference, and why does combining them generate 16 Inter-Layer Dependencies between GAP and LL?
question_variants: Should we use a different, newer version of the Controller Subsystem QDID for the same module?
Why does Including this Host Stack QDID with this Controller QDID create GAP-LL IDLs?
Should we apply for a TCW to cover the GAP-LL Inter-Layer Dependency, or change which QDID we reference?
Is mixing a v5.2 Controller QDID with a v5.4 Host Stack QDID a problem?
actual_issue: The customer's registration quote request referenced a Controller Subsystem QDID at an older Core spec version and a Host Stack + Profile QDID at a newer Core spec version for the same module family; Including both together generated 16 Inter-Layer Dependencies (IDL) between the GAP and LL layers, and it needed to be determined whether to pursue a waiver for the mismatch or change which QDIDs are referenced.
plain_english_explanation: Each Bluetooth registration QDID is tied to a specific version of the Bluetooth specification. If you mix a Controller-layer registration built on an older spec version with a Host/Profile-layer registration built on a newer one, the newer layer can claim support for capabilities (like newer advertising or audio-channel features) that the older layer's checklist simply has no entry for. The system then can't confirm those layers agree with each other, and flags a long list of dependency conflicts. The fix here wasn't to ask for an exception -- it was to use a Host Stack registration built on the same, matching spec version as the Controller registration, and to also use a more current Controller QDID for the same module rather than an older one.
consultant_answer: Two corrections to the quote request: first, the Controller Subsystem QDID listed is a Core spec v5.0 registration; an already-registered v5.2 QDID exists for the same module and should be used instead. Second, the Host Stack + Profile QDID listed (a v5.4 Bluetooth Stack QDID) generates 16 Inter-Layer Dependencies between GAP and LL when Included together with the recommended v5.2 Controller QDID. The root cause: the v5.4 Bluetooth Stack's GAP supports Isochronous and advanced Advertising capabilities added in Core spec v5.3/v5.4, and the v5.2-compliant LL ICS has no corresponding entries for these, so the Consistency Check treats them as 'Support: NO' and flags them as dependency conflicts. Including a same-version v5.2 Bluetooth Stack QDID for the Host Stack + Profile layer instead eliminates the IDL entirely. An earlier message had recommended applying for a TCW (ES-26007) to cover this dependency, but that recommendation is now withdrawn: pairing a lower-version LL with a higher-version GAP is itself an unsound combination, and a TCW request for it is likely to be rejected, making the same-version Host Stack QDID the better path.
decision_logic: An Inter-Layer Dependency between GAP and LL after Including multiple QDIDs should be checked against whether the Included QDIDs were built on different Bluetooth Core spec versions before assuming a waiver (TCW) is the right fix; a newer-spec Host/Profile layer can claim capabilities the older-spec Controller layer's ICS has no entry for, and the more robust fix is to reference a Host Stack QDID built on the same Core spec version as the Controller QDID, rather than to request a waiver for a version mismatch that is unlikely to be approved.
final_recommendation: Reference the already-registered v5.2 Controller Subsystem QDID for this module instead of the v5.0 one listed in the quote request, and reference the matching v5.2 Bluetooth Stack QDID for the Host Stack + Profile layer instead of the v5.4 one, to avoid the GAP-LL Inter-Layer Dependency entirely; do not pursue the previously-suggested TCW (ES-26007) for this mismatch.
risk_if_done_wrong: Proceeding with the originally-requested v5.0 Controller QDID and v5.4 Host Stack QDID combination would leave 16 unresolved Inter-Layer Dependencies in the registration; pursuing a TCW to waive a version mismatch that is itself an unsound pairing carries a high risk of rejection, delaying the registration.
